nameStory: The Boreal Combfoot gets its name from two key features: 'boreal' refers to its northern distribution in the cool forests of Canada and the northern United States, while 'combfoot' describes the tiny comb-like bristles on its hind legs. These special bristles work like little combs to help the spider manipulate and throw sticky silk threads when building its tangled webs.
description: The Boreal Combfoot is a small, dark spider that builds irregular, tangled webs in quiet corners and crevices. Like other false widow spiders, it has a somewhat bulbous abdomen and relatively thin legs, giving it a compact appearance. These spiders typically measure about 1/4 to 1/2 inch in body length, with females being noticeably larger than males. Despite being called a 'false widow,' it's much smaller and less robust-looking than a true black widow spider.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds messy, three-dimensional cobwebs that feel sticky and irregular when accidentally walked through, often found in protected corners or under overhangs

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact spider with a rounded, somewhat swollen abdomen and thin legs that feel delicate if gently touched with a stick

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider, roughly the size of a pea to a grape, with females noticeably plumper than the smaller, more slender males

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down in its web and vibrates rapidly when disturbed, creating a blurring motion that's hard to follow with your eyes

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally dark brown to blackish coloration, often with subtle lighter markings that may be difficult to see without close inspection

habitat: Look for Boreal Combfoots in cool, shaded areas throughout New England's forests and wooded residential areas. They prefer building their webs under log piles, in rock crevices, around building foundations, and in other sheltered spots that stay relatively humid. These spiders thrive in the mixed deciduous and coniferous forests common throughout New England, especially in areas with plenty of leaf litter and natural debris.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and begin rebuilding webs in sheltered areas. Look for fresh, sticky cobwebs appearing in corners and crevices.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible in their webs. This is the best time to observe their characteristic upside-down hanging posture and web-shaking behavior.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and females may be seen guarding egg sacs in their webs. Spiders begin seeking more protected overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults hide in deep crevices, under bark, or in other protected spots. Webs may persist but appear abandoned and collect debris.

funFact: When threatened, the Boreal Combfoot will actually 'throw' sticky silk at potential predators using those special comb bristles on its back legs, essentially lassoing enemies with silk strands before they can get too close!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its cousin, the Triangulate Combfoot, which has distinctive zigzag markings on its abdomen like tiny lightning bolts. Remember: if you can clearly see triangular or chevron patterns, it's the Triangulate Combfoot; if the markings are subtle or hard to make out, you're likely looking at a Boreal Combfoot.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'false widow' often causes unnecessary alarm, but these spiders are not dangerous to humans and are actually beneficial pest controllers. Unlike true black widows, false widows are much smaller, less venomous, and rarely bite humans even when handled.
compareHints: Among New England's false widow spiders, the Boreal Combfoot is most similar to the False Black Widow but is typically smaller and lacks the distinctive glossy, jet-black coloration. It's also easily distinguished from the Triangulate Combfoot by its lack of clear triangular markings, and from the White-spotted False Widow by its absence of obvious light spots or patches on the abdomen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's false widows, the Triangulate Combfoot is the only one with clear triangular markings on the abdomen.

Among its Steatoda relatives in New England, the False Black Widow is the largest and darkest, lacking the distinctive white triangular markings of the Triangulate Combfoot or the white spots of the White-spotted False Widow.

Among its false widow relatives in New England, the White-spotted False Widow is distinguished by its clear white markings, while the Triangulate Combfoot has chevron or zigzag patterns, and the False Black Widow is usually larger and darker with less distinct markings.

Among New England's false widows, the Rabbit Hutch Spider is distinguished by its brownish coloration and the specific pale line pattern on its abdomen - the broken center line plus the cross-line create a unique signature.
The Noble False Widow is the largest and most robust of the false widow species, with a more distinctly bulbous abdomen than the Triangulate Combfoot or False Black Widow.
